# Safety, Privacy, and Deployment

::: {.callout-question}

What does it take to put this in a home, responsibly?

:::

In the lab a failure is a number that dips. In a home it is an arm left mid
motion when the loop hangs, or a week of a child's living room sitting on a
server somewhere. The robot does not get more capable when you ship it. It gets
more exposed, and so does the family.

Two questions decide whether it is ready, and neither is about accuracy. What
happens when it fails? And what leaves the device? This chapter is how you answer
both with a number, and refuse to ship until the numbers pass.

## Deployment is a gate, not a launch

Safety, privacy, and reliability have run as threads through every chapter. Here
they bind at once, and they bind the way [the elements](the-elements.qmd) said
budgets do: you ship only if every one of them closes. A fast, accurate,
power-thrifty robot that cannot reach a safe state when it hangs is not ready. A
flawless one that streams the nursery to the cloud is not ready either. There is
no average to hide in. Deployment is the budget identity again, with the stakes
raised from a missed frame to a child's safety and a family's privacy.

::: {.column-margin}
**Properties in tension**: safety, privacy, and reliability, all binding at once.
No average to hide in.
:::

Two gates decide it, each with a number you measure and defend before shipping.

## The fail-safe: a number for "what happens when it fails"

A wrong or late prediction in a body moves something. The defense is not a better
model; it is a path to a safe state that does not depend on the model being
right. A watchdog watches the loop, and when the loop stops meeting its deadline
or returns garbage, the watchdog takes over and drives the system somewhere safe:
motors to zero torque, the head to neutral, capture off. The number that matters
is how long that takes:

$$\underbrace{t_\text{detect} + t_\text{act}}_{t_\text{recover}} + t_\text{brake} \le t_\text{harm}$$

The body has to come to rest before it can do harm. That budget on the right, the
time from a fault to the first harm, is what functional-safety standards call the
process safety time, and the whole sequence has to fit inside it: detecting the
fault, commanding the stop, and the full braking time the body needs to come to
rest, because safety means stopped before the hazard, not merely slowing, a
deliberately conservative bound. The
distance the body covers over that time is the action chapter's margin; time and
distance are the same constraint in two units. A stuck arm that
reaches a safe stop in 80 milliseconds is safe at speeds where one that takes a
full second is not. You design the watchdog to that process safety time, the same
way the loop was designed to the world's timescale, and you measure the recovery
time rather than assume it.

## The privacy gate: a number for "what leaves the device"

The second gate is the device boundary, and the number is bytes. @fig-egress
draws it. Most of what the robot senses is a firehose, raw audio and video at tens
of megabytes a second, and almost none of it should ever leave the device. What
crosses the boundary is a deliberate, audited trickle: a derived event, a count, a
preference, measured in bytes, never the raw signal it came from.

::: {#fig-egress fig-cap="**The privacy gate**: the raw sensor firehose stays on the device, and only small derived events cross the boundary; the egress audit is the count of what actually crosses, in bytes." fig-alt="Three nested boxes, device inside home network inside cloud. The device holds raw audio and video at about 28 megabytes a second, which stays in. A single arrow crosses a marked privacy gate and carries only a small derived event of about 40 bytes out toward the cloud."}
![](../assets/diagrams/data-egress.svg)
:::

The egress audit is the practice of proving this rather than claiming it: you
watch the device's network boundary and account for every byte that crosses, then
ask of each whether it had to. The default is that raw signal never leaves, and
every exception is a decision someone made and can defend. Privacy by design is
not a policy document. It is a number you can show a parent.

## Build

::: {.callout-build title="Run the ship or no-ship gate"}

Two measurements, both against a threshold you set in advance.

First, the fail-safe. Inject the failure you cannot allow: kill the model
mid-loop, or feed it garbage, and time how long until the system reaches its safe
state. Real failure is unsafe to stage on hardware, so do it in simulation or on a
bench rig with the motors unloaded, and treat the result as your recovery budget.

Second, the egress audit. Run the robot for an hour and capture everything it
sends past the device boundary. Total the bytes, sort them by kind, and mark any
raw signal that escaped. The target for raw signal is zero.

Ship only if recovery time is under the harm threshold and the egress audit holds
no surprises. Write the two numbers and the decision down; that record is the
deployment gate.

:::

## What the number says

The recovery time is almost always longer than the watchdog's own latency,
because detection is the slow part: deciding the loop has truly failed, rather
than merely paused, takes evidence, and evidence takes time. The egress audit
almost always finds something you did not expect leaving, a debug log, a crash
report, a thumbnail, which is exactly why you audit rather than trust the design.
Neither result is a verdict on the robot's intelligence. Both are the price of
putting it in a room with a person, and paying it is what makes the deployment
responsible rather than merely working.

## Read

The fail-safe is the watchdog and safe-state pattern from functional safety, where
a system is designed to fail into a defined safe condition rather than an
undefined one. The privacy gate is data minimization and local-first design: keep
computation and raw data on the device, and let only the smallest necessary
derivative leave. Both are old disciplines; what physical AI adds is that the
failure moves a body and the data is gathered in a home, so the cost of skipping
either is no longer abstract.

::: {.callout-teaching}

- **Hook**: the egress audit. Have students prove what does and does not leave the
  device, and watch the surprise when something unexpected shows up in the
  capture.
- **Open question**: place this chapter last, or thread privacy and safety from
  the first chapter onward? They are constraints on earlier design, not a
  bolt-on, so at minimum they must be foreshadowed throughout.
- **Watch**: keep both gates quantitative. "We take safety seriously" is not a
  number; time to safe state and bytes egressed are.

:::
